title: My Grandmother and I
bodyHtml:
Pronouns are words like us or she that refer to a person or group relevant to the conversation. This problem is about the system of pronouns in the language Lardil, which is spoken on Mornington Island, off the north coast of Australia. Lardil's pronoun system may seem complex at first, but it is organized around a systematic and logical set of principles.

Below are thirteen groups of people, followed by pronouns that could refer to them in Lardil. Note that the Lardil words are not translations of the English—they are pronouns that could refer to the group described in English, similar to how the English pronoun us is not defined as "Alex and me" but might refer to "Alex and me" in a particular context. The English and Lardil are in the same order as each other, not scrambled.

EnglishLardil
my grandmother and Inyarri
he, his brother, and his sisterbili
you, your sister, and your grandsonkili
my great-grandfather and Inyaanki
you and your brotherkirri
my grandparents and Inyali
you and your auntnyiinki
you, your father, and your motherkilmu
my son, my mother, and Inyalmu
she and her grandparentsbili
my son and Inyaanki
my sister, my grandson, and Inyali
she and her great-granddaughterniinki

H1. Match up the following groups and pronouns:

a. you and your parents1. nyalmu
b. my grandfather and I2. bili
c. you and your grandchildren3. kilmu
d. she, her grandmother, and her brother4. kili
e. he and his sister5. nyarri
f. my daughter, my mother, and I6. birri

H2. What would be the correct Lardil pronoun for:

  1. my father and I
  2. you and your granddaughter
  3. my uncle, my aunt, and I
  4. he and his parents
  5. she and her mother
  6. you and your cousin

H3. Circle all of the following groups that would be designated as birri. The number of answers that should be circled could be 0, 1, 2, or 3.

  • my uncle and I
  • you, your brother, and your grandfather
  • she and her sister

H4. There is another pair of pronouns in Lardil, ngakuli and ngakulmu, which are used to refer to groups made of "you, I, and one other person." Assuming that "I" and "you" are brother and sister, which word would you use to refer to:

  1. you, I, and our grandfather
  2. you, I, and our aunt

H5. What Lardil word would refer to "you and I", where "I" refers to the speaker and "you" refers to the speaker's sister?

Lardil also has ngakuli and ngakulmu, used for groups made of "you, I, and one other person." Assuming "I" and "you" are brother and sister, which word would you use?

questions.promptHtml: What Lardil word would refer to "you and I", where "I" refers to the speaker and "you" refers to the speaker's sister?

hints.text: Sort the thirteen examples into groups first by which English pronoun starts the description ("I", "you", "he/she"), and then by how many people are in the group. Two examples that look alike in English can still get different Lardil words, so a third factor must be hiding in the family relationships.

Each Lardil pronoun encodes three things at once: the person (first, second, third), whether the group has exactly two members or more than two, and whether everybody in the group belongs to the same alternate-generation set. Count generational steps: a sibling or cousin is 0 steps away, a parent or child 1 step, a grandparent or grandchild 2 steps. An even number of steps puts you in the same set; an odd number puts you in the other set.

Try it on a line that is not asked about. "she and her grandparents" is third person, has more than two members, and a grandparent is two generational steps away, so everyone is in the same set — and the data gives bili. Compare "you, your father, and your mother": second person, more than two, but a parent is one step away, so the set is mixed, and the data gives kilmu. The endings -li and -lmu are doing that last job.

explanationHtml:
What the pronouns have to say

English pronouns tell you two things: person (am I talking about myself, about you, or about someone else?) and number (one or more than one). Lardil pronouns tell you three things. The third one is the interesting part.

Step 1: split by person

Look at how each Lardil word begins.

  • Groups that include the speaker ("I"): nyarri, nyaanki, nyali, nyalmu — all start with nya-.
  • Groups that include the addressee but not the speaker ("you"): kirri, kili, kilmu and also nyiinki.
  • Groups of other people only ("he/she"): bili, niinki.

The odd ones out are nyaanki, nyiinki, niinki. Notice they line up as a neat set of their own: nyaanki is used for "me + one other", nyiinki for "you + one other", niinki for "her + one other". So the person is marked by the vowel there (nyaa-, nyii-, nii-), and this whole set must be doing a job that the -rri set does not.

Step 2: split by size

Every group in the data with exactly two people gets nyarri, kirri, nyaanki, nyiinki or niinki. Every group with three people gets nyali, kili, bili, nyalmu or kilmu. So Lardil distinguishes dual (exactly two) from plural (three or more), which English does not.

Step 3: the hidden third factor — moiety

Now compare two "you + one person" pairs:

  • you and your brother = kirri
  • you and your aunt = nyiinki

Same person, same size, different word. The difference is the family relationship. A brother is in your own generation; an aunt is in your parents' generation. Many Australian societies divide everyone into two alternating generation sets, called moieties. You are in the same moiety as your siblings and cousins (0 generations away), as your grandparents and grandchildren (2 generations away), and as your great-great-grandparents (4 away). You are in the other moiety from your parents, children, aunts and uncles (1 away) and from your great-grandparents and great-grandchildren (3 away). Even number of steps: same moiety. Odd number: different moiety.

Check it: "my great-grandfather and I" is 3 steps, so mixed, and it gets nyaanki — the same word as "my son and I" (1 step, also mixed). "My grandmother and I" is 2 steps, same moiety, and gets nyarri. It all fits.

The full grid

dual, same moietydual, mixedplural, same moietyplural, mixed
includes "I"nyarrinyaankinyalinyalmu
includes "you"kirrinyiinkikilikilmu
others onlybirriniinkibilibilmu

Two of these cells (birri, bilmu) never appear in the given data — you predict them from the pattern, and the problem asks you to use both.

Working the questions

H1. "You and your parents" is second person, three people, and parents are one step away, so it is plural mixed: kilmu. "He and his sister" is third person, dual, same moiety: the predicted birri. "My daughter, my mother, and I" is first person, plural, and both relatives are one step away from me, so mixed: nyalmu. Careful with "she, her grandmother, and her brother": grandmother is 2 steps and brother 0 steps, so everyone is in the same moiety — bili, not the mixed form.

H2. "He and his parents" is the cell no example filled in: third person, plural, mixed, so bilmu. "You and your cousin" is dual and a cousin is 0 steps away, so same moiety: kirri — the same word as "you and your granddaughter", because a granddaughter is 2 steps away.

H3. birri means third person, dual, same moiety. "My uncle and I" fails on person (it includes the speaker). "You, your brother, and your grandfather" fails on both person and size. Only "she and her sister" fits.

H4 and H5. ngaku- is a fourth person category for groups containing both "you" and "I", and it takes the very same endings. If you and I are brother and sister we are in one moiety; adding our grandfather (2 steps) keeps everyone in that moiety, so the plural same-moiety ending -li gives ngakuli. Adding our aunt (1 step) makes the group mixed, so the plural mixed ending -lmu gives ngakulmu. For just you and me, siblings, that is a group of exactly two in one moiety, so the dual same-moiety ending -rri gives ngakurri.
